newsitem.title: USA: Railroads ready to restart UPS loads after strike.
newsitem.headline: Railroads ready to restart UPS loads after strike.

text.p: The railroads are hoping to restart shipments for United Parcel Service, some as early as Thursday, after UPS and the Teamsters agreed to end a 15-day strike at the world's largest parcel delivery company.

UPS, which told the Federal Reserve Board last week that it is the railroad industry's largest corporate customer, was moving less than three percent of its normal railroad volume during the strike, said UPS spokesman John Flick.
"We have had a huge effect on the railroads," Flick said.

He said UPS provided more than $600 million in revenue to the rail industry in 1996. The company ships 12 million packages a day and moves the vast majority -- 10.4 million packages -- by ground transport via rail and trucks.
"We are still moving a trickle on the rails, but we will not know the full impact for about a week," Flick said Tuesday.
Some railroads said, however, that they did not expect the strike to significantly affect their revenues. Others had not calculated the effect or declined to comment.
"At this point we have yet to make a full determination of the impact on revenues or earnings," Burlington Northern Santa Fe Corp spokesman Jim Sabourin said.

Burlington Northern saw its UPS loads fall from 1,000 to 1,200 a day to about 50 during the strike. Sabourin said UPS loads represent about three percent of the railroad's intermodal revenues, which were just over $2 billion in fiscal 1996.
Intermodal revenues are generated from the movement of trailers and containers filled with merchandise carried by shippers such as UPS.
Norfolk Southern, which handles about 3,500 intermodal loads a day, was down about 100 loads a day during the last days of the strike, spokeswoman Susan Terpay said.
Terpay said the railroad does not foresee an impact on yearly revenues but that it had not estimated the effect, if any, on quarterly results.

Union Pacific spokesman John Bromley declined to comment on the strike's financial impact. He said Union Pacific handles about 700 to 800 UPS loads a day and that during the strike those loads dropped to "virtually none."
Union Pacific moved 384,000 intermodal shipments in fiscal 1996, and UPS is the railroad's fourth largest intermodal customer, Bromley said.
Conrail, which is being acquired by CSX and Norfolk Southern, would not provide details of the strike on its operations.
CSX Corp spokesman Dan Murphy said the strike should have a "negligible" effect on CSX third quarter earnings, even though UPS is its second largest intermodal customer.
Murphy said UPS shipments should begin to pick up almost immediately after the strike ends.
"We'll have more and more freight every day. I think we'll be back up to normal levels by the early part of next week. It all depends on UPS. We're ready," he said.
